analysis.investment_thesis: Data Patterns is an excellent defense electronics franchise — but the Magic Formula is ruthless about price, and the earnings yield of only 1.52% (EBIT 296 Cr / EV 19,530 Cr) is catastrophically below any threshold of attractiveness. Paying EV/EBITDA of 60x for a 708 Cr revenue company means you need flawless execution for a decade just to break even on a value basis.
key_strengths: Revenue CAGR of 31.6% (FY22-FY25) and operating margin of 43% reflect a genuinely scarce, high-moat defense electronics capability
Debt-free balance sheet (6 Cr debt, zero leverage) is excellent capital discipline for a capital-intensive defense R&D business
ROIC on tangible capital is ~20% (EBIT 296 Cr / invested capital ~1,476 Cr) — the business quality is real
key_risks: Earnings yield of only 1.52% means you're paying 66x EBIT — Magic Formula requires >12% yield; this is 8x too expensive
FCF is negative in FY25 (-196 Cr free cash flow) and irregular (only 2/4 years positive) — defense contracts create lumpy working capital cycles
Revenue of only 708 Cr at a 19,562 Cr market cap gives P/S of 20x — any execution stumble or order delay would be devastating
red_flags: Negative OCF in FY25 (-90 Cr) on 222 Cr net profit — cash is not converting; receivables from government orders are likely bloating working capital
CWIP is not a major issue here, but capex nearly tripled from 38 Cr (FY22) to 106 Cr (FY25) — the company is investing ahead of revenues, which is fine but creates execution risk
analysis.detailed_analysis: EV = Market Cap 19,562 + Debt 6 - Cash 38 = 19,530 Cr. EBIT (Operating Income FY25) = 296 Cr → Earnings Yield = 1.52%. This single number says everything. The Magic Formula requires both a cheap price AND a good business — Data Patterns has the good business but the price makes it uninvestable by my framework. For context, at a more reasonable earnings yield of 10%, the stock would need to be priced around 520-540 Cr market cap, implying a ~97% decline from today. The growth story may well play out, but that's a speculation on future earnings, not a value investment. The negative FCF in FY25 on strong reported earnings is a classic defense-sector working capital trap that concerns me.
